record.paper_title: Open Problems Related to Quantum Query Complexity
record.original_question: Does there exist an oracle, possibly even a quantum oracle consisting of unitary transformations provided as black boxes, relative to which QMA differs from QMA(2), where QMA(2) is the analogue of QMA with two unentangled Merlins and Arthur may assume that the witness state is a tensor product across two polynomial-size registers?

evidence.quote: In 2007, Greg Kuperberg and I [8] at least showed that there’s a quantum oracle U—that is, a collection of unitary transformations provided as black boxes—such that QMAU̸= QCMAU.
Problem 2 Is there an oracle—even a quantum oracle—relative to which QMA̸= QMA (2)?

Here, QMA (2) is the analogue of QMA to allow two unentangled Merlins, so that Arthur can always assume that the witness state he receives is a tensor product |ψ⟩⊗| ϕ⟩ across two polynomial-size registers.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Define the complexity class QMA (Quantum Merlin–Arthur) as the class of promise problems for which there exists a polynomial-time quantum verifier V such that: on input x of length n, V receives a quantum witness state |ψ⟩ on poly(n) qubits from an all-powerful prover (Merlin), and (i) if x is a yes-instance, there exists |ψ⟩ such that V accepts (x,|ψ⟩) with probability ≥ 2/3; (ii) if x is a no-instance, then for all |ψ⟩, V accepts with probability ≤ 1/3.

Define QMA(2) analogously, except that the witness is required to be a tensor product |ψ⟩ ⊗ |ϕ⟩ of two states on poly(n)-qubit registers supplied by two non-communicating, unentangled Merlins; completeness and soundness are defined as in QMA but quantifying over product states.

For an oracle O (which may be a classical oracle, or more generally a quantum oracle, i.e., a family of unitary transformations acting on poly(n) qubits accessible as black boxes to the verifier), let QMA^O and QMA(2)^O denote the analogous classes when the verifier is given oracle access to O.

Question: Does there exist an oracle O (possibly a quantum/unitary oracle) such that QMA^O ≠ QMA(2)^O?
artifact.status_search_result: No oracle separation between QMA and QMA(2), classical or quantum, is known. Recent literature on related oracle separations (e.g., QMA vs QCMA, UniqueQMA vs QMA) explicitly notes that no quantum oracle separation between QMA(2) and QMA has been established and that no natural candidate problem is known. The problem appears to remain open as of 2026.

status_evidence.title: UniqueQMA vs QMA: oracle separation and eigenstate thermalization hypothesis
status_evidence.snippet: Recent work on oracle separations within the QMA family; no QMA vs QMA(2) oracle separation cited.
status_evidence.claim: As of late 2024, no oracle separation between QMA and QMA(2) is established.

status_evidence.title: A distribution testing oracle separation between QMA and QCMA
status_evidence.snippet: Establishes oracle separations within the QMA/QCMA hierarchy, but does not address QMA vs QMA(2).
status_evidence.claim: Recent oracle-separation results focus on QMA vs QCMA, leaving QMA vs QMA(2) open.

status_evidence.title: Quantum Versus Classical Proofs and Advice (Aaronson–Kuperberg)
status_evidence.snippet: Foundational reference for quantum oracle separations involving QMA; mentions related open questions.
status_evidence.claim: Oracle separations involving QMA(2) remain among the open questions in quantum complexity.
